git add src/server.js src/server.test.js public/index.html data/README.md && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(logo): redirect placeholder brands to the icon their own site declares

- Look up <link rel="icon"> on the site of each placeholder,yes brand in brands.csv, cached
- Fall back to the service URL when the site has no https icon or fails
- Widen CSP img-src to https: so redirects to brand-hosted icons load
- Listen only when run directly, and test iconFromHtml
- Note in data/README.md that /logo reads the own column
EOF
git log --stat -1 | cat && git status --short

result:
`/logo` now sends placeholder brands to the icon their own site declares, and the change is committed as `c5077d7`. The unit test passes. I also ran the real server with `fetch` stubbed out: a site with a declared icon got redirected to it and was fetched only once, while a site with no icon, a 404 or a dead site fell back to the placeholder.

Files written:
- `src/server.js`
- `src/server.test.js` (new)
- `public/index.html`
- `data/README.md`

Decisions I made:
- **Which brands:** only the 7 marked `placeholder,yes` in `brands.csv` get the fallback. The other 69 placeholder brands were checked by hand as having no usable icon, so redirecting them would swap a placeholder for a broken image. Limiting the lookup to these 7 also stops the server from fetching arbitrary sites via `/logo?domain=`.
- **Security policy:** the page's CSP only allowed images from itself and the icon service, so the browser would have blocked a redirect to a brand's site. I widened `img-src` to any `https:` address, because a brand's icon can live on another host such as `www.` or a CDN.
- **Caching:** each brand's icon is cached until the server restarts. Failed lookups are retried, and only `https` icons are used.

I skipped decoding HTML entities other than `&` and handling a page's `<base href>`; that's worth adding if a brand's icon doesn't resolve. The server now only listens when run directly (`npm start`), so the test can import it without opening a port.

Port 3000 on IPv4 is already taken by an unrelated `bun` process on your machine, so I ran my checks over IPv6 and left that process alone.
